001: So, first week at the company, how do you find the general atmosphere?
Honestly, I'm pleasantly surprised. People are very open, but I still have to figure out some unspoken habits.
What do you mean, for example?
Well, here, everyone seems to eat lunch together at noon, and I feel like it's almost a mandatory ritual.
Oh yes, it's a real moment of team bonding. That's where a lot of informal things get settled.
I see, I'll get on board starting tomorrow then. Thanks for the tip.
002: How did your meeting with the marketing team go?
It was interesting, but I noticed they don't like being given overly direct instructions.
Yes, they prefer that you suggest ideas and let them validate things themselves.
It's a consensus culture, in a way. I'm going to have to adapt my management style.
Exactly. And above all, avoid criticizing an idea in public, they take it very badly.
Thanks for the heads up, I'll be careful with the delivery as much as the content.
003: Did you see the director's email about the new schedules?
Yes, I read it, but I find the wording pretty ambiguous. Does it apply to everyone?
I think it only applies to the project teams, but nobody dares to ask him for clarification.
That's typical here, people prefer to interpret rather than ask questions that might cause trouble.
That's kind of the company culture, yes. But if you ask me, a clarification email wouldn't hurt.
You're right, I'll write to him politely to clear up the doubt.
004: I get the feeling that French employees go back and forth a lot between work life and personal life.
That's true, and it's quite different from what I've experienced elsewhere. Here, people don't stay late on principle.
And above all, you don't show that you're overwhelmed, it's frowned upon. You have to maintain a certain composure.
It's a form of professional discretion, in a way. I need to learn to manage my workload without complaining.
Exactly, but you also need to know how to say no when it's too much. It's a subtle balance.
I'll try to find the right middle ground. Thanks for these insights.
005: Did you see how Paul presented his project in the meeting? He was very direct.
Yes, and I could feel that it kind of put the management committee on edge.
That's exactly what I was telling you: here, you always have to soften things and offer several options.
I understand better now why my colleagues use so many conditionals in their presentations.
It's a form of professional politeness. It leaves an easy way out for everyone.
I'm going to practice adopting this more diplomatic style.
006: How do you find the internal communication at the company?
It's very rich, almost too much. I get dozens of emails a day, it's hard to prioritize.
Yes, it's a real problem here. But there's an unwritten rule: anything important goes through the phone or in person.
Really? So emails are more of a written record than a decision-making tool?
Exactly. If you want to move a project forward, it's better to go see people directly.
I'll change the way I work then. Thanks for this valuable tip.
007: Have you noticed that meetings often start ten minutes late?
Yes, and I admit it throws me off a bit. Back home, we were very strict about punctuality.
Here, it's a sign of flexibility. But careful, never be late for a client appointment.
So it's a matter of context. You have to know how to adapt to who you're dealing with.
Exactly, that's the whole art of professional diplomacy in this company.
I'm starting to understand the codes, little by little.
008: I have a doubt about how to address management. Can I use the informal "tu" with the director?
No, absolutely not. Here, we systematically use the formal "vous" with members of the management committee.
Even if they use "tu" with us first?
Yes, it's a sign of hierarchical respect. You only cross that line after years of working together.
It's a real social boundary then. I'll stick with the formal form to avoid any blunders.
That's safer, yes. And it shows that you've picked up on the company's codes.
009: How is your integration into the sales team going?
It's going well, but I'm a bit surprised by the internal competition among colleagues.
Yes, it's a fairly individualistic culture here, even though everyone pretends to be supportive.
That's an interesting paradox. So you have to show your results while cultivating a team image.
Exactly, it's a subtle balance between individual performance and collective spirit.
I'll try to play that double game smartly.
010: Do you have any plans for the long weekend?
Yes, I'm going to take the opportunity to completely disconnect. I've noticed that's important here.
That's true, disconnecting is highly valued here. No one will send you emails on Sunday.
That's a good thing, but it takes real discipline not to bring your work home.
It's a matter of organization, but also of trust in your team.
I'll stick to it, it's essential to last in the long run at this company.
